title: There or not there? A multidisciplinary review and research agenda on the impact of transparent barriers on human perception, action, and social behavior

findings.antecedent: Transparent barriers (e.g., large, frameless glass panels)
findings.quote: Unsurprisingly, undetected transparent barriers can pose a serious health and safety risk.

findings.antecedent: Specific luminance differences between neighboring parts of a surface
findings.quote: Metelli demonstrated that specific luminance differences between neighboring parts of a surface would induce the impression that some parts were seen directly, whereas others were seen through a transparent layer.
contours aligned in the way of an X-junction (see Figure 3B) indicate transparency

findings.antecedent: Conflicting tactile and visual information (e.g., transparent barrier physically blocks but visually allows access)
findings.consequent: Reliance on visual information for peripersonal space representation
findings.quote: Initial evidence indicates that when faced with conflicting information coming from tactile and visual sensors, humans rely more strongly on the latter, especially when the sensory contradictions arise within a person's peripersonal space

findings.antecedent: Transparent barrier between perceiver and approaching object/person
findings.consequent: Rapid startle and withdrawal responses (as if no barrier was present)
findings.quote: people can be fully aware of being protected from collisions or touch by a transparent wall, yet simultaneously show rapid responses to approaching objects or people as if no wall was present.

The first study on distance estimation, for instance, revealed that preschoolers exaggerated distances between objects separated by both opaque as well as transparent barriers, whereas adults only exaggerated distances across opaque barriers (Kosslyn et al., 1974). A subsequent study demonstrated that neither adults, nor school-aged children overestimated distances between objects separated by transparent barriers (Herman et al., 1987).

findings.antecedent: Transparent barriers (especially for young children and individuals with cognitive decline)
findings.consequent: Ability to navigate and interact with the environment (e.g., detour, opening doors, crossing walkways)
findings.quote: These data demonstrate that negotiating transparent materials is developmentally dependent on interacting with them.

findings.antecedent: Physical separation by transparent barriers (vs. opaque or no barrier)
findings.consequent: Impact on social behavior (e.g., interpersonal distance, privacy, crowding, territoriality)
findings.quote: Given that the exchange of visual information remains unimpaired, to which extent does a separation of strangers by a transparent barrier impact social behavior?

findings.antecedent: Spaces largely defined by transparent barriers
findings.quote: Their visual permeability, however, may reduce a person's sense of confinement (Stamps, 2010). As a result, the same density level may reduce feelings of crowding in spaces largely defined by transparent barriers than in spaces defined by non-transparent barriers.

findings.antecedent: Views through transparent barriers (e.g., to nature vs. built environments)
findings.consequent: Stress reduction/induction and readiness to aggress/withdraw
findings.quote: Thus, a person's readiness to aggress against social threats encountered indoors may get reduced or amplified, depending on whether transparent barriers afford stress-reducing or stress-inducing views

findings.antecedent: Lighting conditions around transparent barriers (e.g., brighter rooms)
findings.consequent: Social inhibition, anti-social behavior, prosocial behavior
findings.quote: Brighter rooms, for instance, seem to facilitate social inhibition (Hirsh et al., 2011), an effect that can reduce anti-social behavior (such as aggression or dishonesty, see Page and Moss, 1976; Prentice-Dunn and Rogers, 1980; Zhong et al., 2010) but also prosocial behavior (such as the willingness to collaborate, see Steidle et al., 2013).

findings.antecedent: Windowed view to a natural setting (vs. brick wall) for surgical patients
findings.quote: The results showed faster, less painful recovery for surgical patients with a windowed view to a natural setting than for those with a view of a brick wall.

findings.antecedent: Open plan offices with transparent barriers (e.g., for visual connection but acoustic separation)
findings.quote: Open plan designs generally aim to optimize communication and information flow across individuals. Yet, their practical implementation is frequently accompanied by complaints about privacy violations
